key_insight: Higher urinary cadmium was associated with shorter survival, with the largest absolute differences at the earliest conditional survival quantile.
clinical_relevance: The findings support population-level cadmium exposure reduction, but do not establish causality or guide individual treatment.
method: Linked NHANES 1999–2014 data for 24,338 US adults aged 40 or older to mortality records through 2019.
Used weighted censored quantile regression to assess survival at the 10th, 25th, and 50th percentiles, adjusting for confounders across five imputations.
Examined blood lead and mercury and urinary cadmium and arsenic; urinary-metal analyses required preserved kidney function.
evidence_signal: Among 7,061 participants in the cadmium analysis, each doubling of urinary cadmium was associated with 1.71–1.92 years shorter conditional survival at the 10th percentile versus 1.35–1.53 years at the median.
watch_item: This observational environmental-health study—not AI cancer drug discovery—remains vulnerable to residual confounding, and some median survival estimates were not estimable.
paper_title: Environmental toxic metal exposure and conditional mortality survival among US adults: a prospective cohort study
